sections.title: Listening and dialogue: communication that enables us to lead together

blocks.html: At its core, leading together depends on the quality of conversation and collective thinking that occurs among team members. This requires moving beyond conventional debate, where participants argue for pre-decided positions, towards genuine dialogue where understanding and collective insight can develop. This collective insight creates a richer, more complex understanding and can build shared ownership before decisions are made.

blocks.name: p56-1
blocks.caption: Different levels of listening by Otto Scharmer

blocks.html: Downloading – listening for what confirms what we already know – keeps us stuck in existing patterns. We appear to be listening to the other person while talking to them to seem polite while, in reality, we are more focused on our own agendas and getting our point across. Factual listening helps us open our mind and stay open to information that challenges our assumptions. We listen for information and facts in what the other person is saying, but also already look for cracks in those facts that we can argue against when it is our time to speak. This way of listening, which often results in debate, is typical in an academic setting. Empathic listening allows us to see from another’s perspective. When utilising this kind of listening, we step out of our own patterns of thinking to listen to the other person with an open heart, putting ourselves in their shoes and understanding their perspective. Generative listening, the deepest level, opens us to emerging possibilities that weren’t present before the conversation began. We can follow the flow of conversation and sense what needs to be said, co-creating with others in a way that helps us expand our own ways of thinking in a generative way. Collaborative leadership requires building the ability for these deeper forms of listening to take place across the organisation.

Distinct from discussion or debate, dialogue creates space for collective thinking. Rather than individuals presenting finished thoughts for approval or rejection, dialogue allows individuals’ ideas to be explored, built upon, and transformed through interaction. Key principles of dialogue include noticing and suspending judgment, making one’s thinking and reasoning process transparent, and allowing enough silence and reflection for new insights to surface.
Dialogue practice

In dialogue practice, as described by David Bohm (1996), a group intentionally practises dialogue to learn this new way of being together. Continuous practice is essential – dialogue is a skill that develops over time through repeated experience. For instance, a group might set aside two hours weekly to practise dialogue.
Setting up a dialogue practice:
Sit in a circle so that participants can see each other (groups of 4 – 20 people work well)
Begin with a brief meditation or silence to help everyone settle into a listening space – ask participants to tune into their bodies, breath, and the space itself
Start the dialogue. In the beginning, we recommend having a facilitator who can help the group slow down and notice the quality of conversation
Guiding principles:

blocks.name: p57-0
blocks.caption: Practising dialogue

blocks.html: Ideally, dialogue has no predefined question or agenda. This allows the conversation to follow what wants to be explored by the group in the moment – different topics can be shared. However, for a first dialogue session, it can be helpful to focus on the topic of dialogue itself: What is dialogue? How is it different from a discussion or debate?
Meta-dialogue:
To learn more, explore these additional resources: Scharmer, C. O. (2018). The Essentials of Theory U: Core Principles and Applications. Berrett-Koehler Publishers.
Bohm, D. (1996). On Dialogue. Routledge.

An important aspect of dialogue is meta-dialogue, that is, the group commenting on the conversation itself. Notice: How spacious does the conversation feel? If people are interrupting, waiting eagerly for their turn to speak, or raising hands, these can be indicators that participants are focused more on speaking than listening. When you notice these patterns, name them, slow down, and invite people to tune back into listening.
Blogpost from Tuff Leadership Training: tuffledarskapstraning.se/article/tanka-tillsammans
A recommended resource for deepening your understanding of this practice is Bohm’s book On Dialogue (1996).
Movement score: group morning exercise on dialoguing (30 min)

As you walk through a space, notice the walls, objects, and other people. Notice your breathing and relax your shoulders and neck and jaw. Release your feet to the ground. Stretch your body parts as you walk. (5 min)

Find a partner. Your partner will move through the space and also up and down. Your task is to follow the height of your partner’s pelvis with your own. That means that when your partner jumps, you jump, and when they move towards the ground, you follow. You might be close to each other or far away in space. The idea is that you become so connected in movement that an outsider would not be able to discern who is leading and who is following. (5 min)
Exchange roles and repeat the exercise. (5 min)

Now, both you and your partner are leaders and followers at the same time. So the leadership role will shift instantaneously. Do this for at least 10 minutes. You might want to put on some background music.
Give each other feedback on how it felt, what the challenges and joys of dancing together were.

sections.title: Building a culture of feedback, coaching and conflict resolution

blocks.html: In traditional hierarchies, feedback and coaching typically flow downwards from managers to employees. Often, feedback and coaching are limited to yearly performance and development reviews, and, at best, such talks occur between managers and employees a few times a year. Collaborative leadership requires a fundamental shift – spreading out these practices so that feedback and coaching flow in all directions, becoming informal, continuous, and built into everyday work. This shift is essential because the responsibility for developing people and holding them accountable can no longer sit with just one manager – it must be shared across the team. As people navigate changing roles and participate in shared decision-making, they need ongoing feedback from their peers to understand how their actions affect others and to develop the group’s collective competence and abilities to work together. This peer feedback also helps people navigate the subtle dynamics of power and participation – understanding when to step forward and when to step back, as well as when they’re contributing productively and when they might be unintentionally dominating or holding back. Without such distributed feedback and coaching, collaborative approaches tend to break down, as people lack the information they need to adjust their behaviour and work better together.

A feedback culture normalises the giving and receiving of observations, reactions, and reflections as a natural part of collaboration. This requires developing specific skills: knowing how to offer feedback that is direct and clear, timely, and comes from a place of wanting to support the person’s growth rather than criticise or blame them. Equally important are skills in receiving feedback – listening to feedback with curiosity rather than defensiveness, and understanding the difference between evaluation and development.

Likewise, addressing conflict directly is critical in collective forms of leadership cultures, where the team must develop the capacity to work through disagreements, tensions, and differing perspectives together. This means learning to name tensions early – when they are still small and manageable – rather than allowing them to accumulate into larger conflicts that damage relationships and undermine trust. It also means distinguishing between different types of conflict: task-related disagreements that can strengthen decision-making versus interpersonal tensions that require relationship repair. Without having skills and processes for addressing conflict, teams default to avoidance, which leads to passive-aggressive behaviour, behind-the-scenes complaints, and the erosion of psychological safety.

Similarly, in collective forms of leadership cultures, coaching shifts from a specialised role to a shared skill. Team members develop the ability to ask powerful questions, listen deeply, and support one another’s growth and problem-solving. Such peer coaching recognises that expertise and wisdom exist throughout the organisation, not just in official leadership positions. For managers in hierarchical organisations, this represents a significant transition. They must shift from solving problems for their employees to supporting people in finding their own solutions through asking questions.
Practices for feedback and coaching
To learn more, explore these additional resources:
Blogpost on feedback: tuffledarskapstraning.se/article/vill-ni-infora-feedbackkultur

Karin Tenelius, an advisor in one of the research projects this book is based on and whose voice you hear from in “Voices from the field”, started the consulting company Tuff Leadership Training. The consultancy helps organisations transition towards self-managing principles and has developed training programmes for coaching, conflict, relationship repair and feedback conversations, offering processes for conversations that strengthen collective forms of leadership, using specific, shared language for teams.
Blogpost on conflict: tuffledarskapstraning.se/article/konflikthantering-pa-arbetsplatsen

For instance, Tuff Leadership Training uses the word pebble to signify small tensions or discomforts. By naming and sharing pebbles early on, team members can address tensions and possible misunderstandings as they arise – deepening authenticity and psychological safety rather than allowing tensions to build up over time.
Practising peer-to-peer feedback

For deeper conflicts or relationship repair, different languages and processes are used. Tuff Leadership Training uses the phrase “moose heads on the table” to signify these bigger tensions that everyone senses but no one is addressing. They have defined processes for relationship repair conversations to work through more substantial conflicts.
The key practice here is developing a shared language and practices that allow your team to engage in different types of conversations.

Karin Tenelius starts with a simple observation: self-organising requires more collaboration, collaboration requires communication, and communication requires a language for things that are usually left unnamed. “Between people, there are interpersonal relationships happening; that’s air, basically. But the air has qualities: moods, tension or not. In a team, there’s a working climate, and you need a completely different language to be able to name what’s going on between people.” Part of what she and her colleagues do when working with teams is help them develop that language.

The examples she gives are small but telling. The word pebble is used to name a friction between two people: something like a stone in your shoe that is tickling or hurting you, that, in most workplaces, would simply be left untouched. “In ordinary workplaces, that friction just goes on for ages; some people don’t talk to each other if they don’t like each other. But in self-organising teams, we have to cooperate, so we need to resolve it.” A moose head is something bigger: a tension that has become infected, perhaps taboo, that everyone in the room senses but nobody is addressing. These invented words do something important. They make it possible to talk about things that previously had no name and therefore no handle.

The core objective of the rituals Karin recommends is to keep the culture open: to maintain an environment where nothing is too small to address and where the working climate is often tended to. Quality check-ins, she stresses, are not about reporting what you did last weekend or announcing that you feel fine. They are about genuinely attending to how people are doing and how they are. Quarterly meetings include a dedicated moment to ask whether any moose heads have surfaced. Feedback is built in as an ongoing practice rather than reserved for formal reviews, with the team developing shared agreements about how to name and address behaviour that is getting in the way. “It’s really about keeping communication and the working climate clean.”

On the question of when and how feedback happens, Karin is pragmatic. Some of it is responsive: if someone is behaving in a way that is not helpful, there needs to be an agreement that a colleague can name it at the moment. Some of it is structural: evaluating after a meeting what worked and what did not, as a regular ritual, so that the team can keep refining how it operates together. Decision-making processes are themselves rituals, she argues, ensuring that mandates are kept where they belong and that before anyone makes a decision that affects others, there is a shared process for doing so. Importantly, she cautions against trying to design all of this in advance. “It’s better to carve out rituals and procedures along the way, as things occur that need to be addressed.”

When teams come from more hierarchical cultures where psychological safety is low, she does not begin by demanding openness. She begins by onboarding people into the idea of it: acknowledging the fear that is present, making it nameable, and letting openness grow from there. “Openness feeds openness,” she says. Most people, in her experience, actually want to be more open. What stands in the way is fear, and fear responds to being named. “Ask: what is it that we don’t talk about? And then openness is created.” On power, her approach is similarly direct. Rather than committing to flattening all hierarchies, she encourages teams to name the hierarchies that actually exist, including knowledge and competence hierarchies, and to talk about them honestly. A founder who holds power by virtue of being a founder needs to acknowledge that explicitly and take responsibility for how it shows up. “It’s resolved through communication,” she says.

sections.title: Talking about power and practising power differently

blocks.html: A challenging cultural shift for collaborative leadership involves naming and changing power dynamics. Traditional organisations often avoid explicit discussion of power, preferring to maintain the false idea that hierarchies are purely functional or based solely on merit. Yet power – formal and informal, visible and invisible – shapes our interactions.

Collaborative leadership requires developing a collective understanding of power: recognising how it operates, acknowledging who holds it in different contexts, and discussing how it’s used. One way to understand and talk about power is to distinguish between four different types: power-over (domination and control); power-under (resistance); power-within (personal agency and self-determination); and power-with (collective capacity and working together as equals). While hierarchical organisations depend primarily on power-over, collaborative leadership aims to develop power-within and power-with.

blocks.name: p62-0
blocks.caption: Different forms of power, adapted from the typology of Starhawk, 1987.

blocks.html: This transformation is not about eliminating all hierarchy or pretending everyone has equal power. Rather, it involves being explicit about where formal authority resides, having clarity about where decisions are made and who holds accountability for them, and ensuring that those most affected by decisions have a meaningful voice in making them. It means recognising when hierarchical decision-making is appropriate and when a more collective form of leadership serves the organisation better.
A practice for exploring different forms of power
Review the model on power (Starhawk, 1987). Individually, reflect on examples for each type of power – how does each one manifest in your life and work?
How do different forms of power feel?

An embodied practice can deepen this reflection: write each power type on a piece of paper or sticky note and place them on the floor. Stand on each paper in turn – how does it feel to stand in each type of power? This embodied layer can add another dimension, helping you recognise how these powers feel in your body and how to recognise them in practice.

After individual exploration, pair up with a colleague and share your examples. This provides a more intimate space for sharing than a large group setting and can be a good way to deepen your understanding of each other.
Finally, come together as a whole group to discuss: How could the team support “power with” and “power within”? What specific practices or changes would strengthen these forms of power?
To learn more, explore these additional resources:
Starhawk (Miriam Simos), 1987. Truth or Dare: Encounters with Power, Authority, and Mystery (the author of the model/ distinction of power)
Rau, Ted J. 2023. Collective Power: Patterns for a Self-Organized Future. Sociocracy For All.

Nati Lombardo, an advisor of one of the research projects this book is based on and whose voice you hear from in “Voices from the field”, is a co-founder of the consulting company The HUM, which helps organisations introduce collective forms of leadership. On their website “Let’s talk about power”, you can find further exercises for exploring power. Visit The Hum’s resource at: thehum.org/visitors/resources. All of their exercises are free; you just need to create a free account first to access them.

Transforming culture in organisations that have long operated as a hierarchy is rarely a question of implementing the right framework or attending the right training. Nati Lombardo, who has worked with NGOs and cooperatives through such transitions, usually starts with something simpler.

“When it comes down to it, our main advice is: talk about it. Just talk about all the things you think you can talk about. Make things explicit. Make space for people to be able to name what they need, what they want, what they’re scared of.” The phrase “bringing your whole self to work” may have become a cliché, she acknowledges, but the underlying idea is genuine. Creating space for people to show up more fully is not a nice addition to cultural change. It is the beginning of it. And that space cannot be designed from above and handed down. It has to be built together, starting from real questions: what does each person in this team need? What do we all bring? What happens when my personality meets yours? “From that place,” she says, “you can decide together what kind of culture you want to have, and then ask: where is the gap between where we are now and where we want to go, and how do we support each other?”

One of the conversations that tends to be hardest to open, particularly in Scandinavian contexts where the word itself carries uncomfortable associations, is the conversation about power. Nati is direct about what makes it possible. “It’s quite important that the people who already hold some of the power, whether social capital or explicit role-based power, are the ones who open up the conversation.” An external facilitator can help create conditions for this, but the key move is modelling: showing, through how you show up, that talking about power is not an accusation or a threat but a necessary part of building something more honest together. Nati recalls a fishbowl exercise in one of her workshops where several participants found it genuinely difficult to acknowledge the power they held, precisely because they associated power with something negative. What changes when more nuance enters that conversation – when power can be talked about in terms of how it is earned, how it can be used well, and how it can be distributed – is that the topic stops being taboo and starts being workable in the team.

That same dynamic, she argues, is at the heart of the most common obstacle she encounters when working with teams on cultural change. You can put the right structures in place, agree on the right values, and run the right workshops, but if the people who hold formal or informal power behave in ways that contradict what is being said, the culture will not shift. “You can talk about a lot of things, but if the person who holds that leadership role shows up in a way that contradicts all of their stated ideals, the culture is really not going to shift, and it will be much more difficult.” Role modeling, she says, is not one ingredient among many. It is the condition that determines whether everything else lands or not.

On a final note, developing a culture for leading together can be challenging – especially as remote and distributed work styles become more common. Online work and geographic separation makes the informal relationship-building that supports trust and psychological safety more difficult due to things like having a more task-based focus and a lack of spontaneous interactions. To navigate these challenges, we recommend experimenting with structures that support teams in building a culture of safety, and that help deepen relationships. This demands prioritising bringing people together for relationship-building, creating explicit agreements about how teams will work together, and continually examining whether the culture and relationships are supported with the actual practices.
A practice for developing team agreement

With your team, discuss your shared purpose and values, and identify which behaviours support these. In the previous chapter on self-leadership, we introduced the Personal Canvas practice. Look at that practice and build upon it, progressing from individual reflections to reflections on team level.

After each team member has created a personal canvas with their own reflections about purpose, values, passions and desired impact, invite everyone to share their thoughts and ask the team to distill core shared values on the team level. How can a team formulate a shared purpose that bridges the individual sense of purpose with a purpose that everyone on the team shares, while also being connected to the overall purpose of organisation? Invite team members to also reflect on what kind of supporting behaviours would be needed on the team to enable them to enact shared purpose in everyday work. Then come together as a whole group to discuss and find a shared understanding of supporting behaviours and how they can be transformed into concrete work principles and activities integrated into the team’s daily work.

You can use sticky notes to capture and cluster ideas, or create a visual collage such as a tree – with roots representing your values, the trunk representing your purpose, and leaves representing the behaviours and activities that bring these to life.
Developing shared values, purpose and desired team activities and behaviours.

Revisit these agreements regularly to ensure they continue to support how you actually work together. You can hang a shared team agreement or manifesto in the team’s shared work space as a daily reminder and to make it more accessible as something you can always easily come back to.

For a structured template to guide a team agreement process, we recommend using The Hum’s How do we want to be together? exercise which can be found at thehum.org/visitors/resources. (It’s free. Create a free account to access it). This exercise provides a framework for creating team agreements that support your collaborative culture.

The practitioners we spoke to have each developed their own answer to the question of what cultural change actually looks like in practice, not as a set of abstract principles but as repeatable ways of being together that teams can build into their daily work.

Mette Aagaard draws heavily on the sociocracy toolbox*, a set of principles and structures she has seen work across very different organisations. “Personally, I find it hard to take part in meetings or dialogue that don’t adhere to these kinds of principles,” she says. The practices are specific and unglamorous, but that is precisely the point.

It starts with the check-in: not a 30 update on what everyone has been doing, but a brief moment to ensure that each person is genuinely present and that nothing is standing in the way of their full attention. Then there is decision-making by consent, which she is an enthusiastic advocate for because it sidesteps the power struggles that tend to emerge from consensus-based processes. Speaking in rounds ensures that talking time is distributed rather than captured by the most confident voices. Having a dedicated facilitator for each meeting means that when something difficult needs to be brought to the table, whether because the content is complex or because emotions are running high, there is someone whose explicit role is to hold the space. “It’s about helping the team refrain from moving into decision-making mode when what we are discussing is not yet ready for a decision, but needs more exploration of perspectives in order to better understand the complexity of an issue.”

Working with roles and how they are distributed and nominated among colleagues is another piece, one she acknowledges can be genuinely sensitive. And then there is transparency, which she finds teams often struggle with in unexpected ways. She describes one team that considered introducing full transparency around the registration of working hours. The idea came from a place of mutual care: without a manager surveying hours, colleagues had no way of knowing if someone was accumulating far too many and needed help or protection. But others experienced the proposal as surveillance. “I don’t want my colleagues to monitor when or how much I’m working, and I feel it becomes a competition for who’s accumulated the most hours, as in who’s the best colleague.” The conversation took a long time and carried a lot of hard feelings. Eventually, they went ahead with it. And what happened was not competition or blaming each other: they discovered that one colleague had been registering fewer hours than she should have been.When they asked what was going on, it turned out she was navigating a difficult situation at home involving a child who was struggling to attend school. “And then the team said: now that we know this, how can we help you?” The transparency that had felt threatening became the condition for support.

Nati Lombardo offers two stories from her own experience that, together, capture something important about what makes this work succeed and what can make it fall apart even when everything seems to be in place.
* sociocracyforall.org/and Sociocracy handbook “Many Voices One Song”: sociocracyforall.org/many-voices-one-song/

The first is the case of Loomio, the organisation where she first began working in this way. By most measures, the conditions were right. The culture was strong, the processes were well designed, and the team had even built their own technology to support their way of working. “We had great processes. We had the technology. We built it ourselves to enable this way of working.” And yet it became unsustainable, not because of anything internal to the culture or the organisation, but because the funding was not there. The income was not being generated. “So it’s like: we can look at all the pieces, but sometimes it’s not just about the culture and how we organise. It’s also about what’s happening in the world. What is the context? How do we pay ourselves?” The lesson Nati draws from Loomio is not a counsel of despair but a reminder that cultural and organisational transformation does not happen in a vacuum. External factors matter, and sometimes, despite everything, you have to let go.

The second story is more hopeful. Working with a cooperative in the UK, Nati encountered a team that had already been on their journey for five or six years by the time she came in to support their decision-making processes. What struck her was not the absence of challenges but the quality of the response to them: a genuine collective willingness to keep improving, keep changing, keep trying rather than giving up. “Everyone was really engaged in what was happening.” The team had a high level of trust, and had built real relationships with each other despite being geographically distributed. They also brought something to their difficulties that cannot be installed through a workshop or framework: the disposition to stay in it together. That, she suggests, is what the culture ultimately needs to make possible.
What are your team’s shared core values and purpose?
How are they connected to the overall values and purpose of your organisation?
What kinds of behaviours are crucial for enacting your team’s shared values and purpose in your daily work?
How do you experience psychological safety in your team?
What small, concrete actions can your team take to strengthen psychological safety?
What is the most common way of listening in your team (downloading, factual, empathic, or generative)?
How can you integrate intentional practice of more empathic and generative listening and dialogue into your daily work and into your team rituals?
How is coaching and the giving and receiving of feedback practised in your team/organisation today?
Does responsibility lie with the manager(s) or is it shared among team colleagues?
How can you develop and integrate peer-to-peer feedback and coaching practices into your team/organisational culture?
How do you deal with conflicts in your team/organisation?
What would it take to build a culture in which you can openly talk about conflict together?
How is power exercised in your team/organisation (formally and informally)?
Can you talk openly about power in your team/organisation? If not, what would need to change to make that possible?
Which forms of power (power-over, power-under, power-within and power-with) would you say are most often exercised in your team/ organisation? In what situations?
How can you strengthen your team/organisation to practise more power-within and power-with?

In this chapter, we introduced different aspects of building a culture for leading together – from psychological safety to deeper levels of generative listening and dialogue. Feedback, coaching, conflict resolution, and distributing power have been discussed as cornerstones for sharing leadership. We argued that creating a culture where team members feel safe to be themselves and experience trust between each other – allowing them to take risks to both try out new things together and bring tough questions to the table – is a crucial condition for developing shared leadership. Teams need to openly discuss and reach a consensus about their shared values and purpose, as well as ways of working together that can support them in enacting their values and following their “why” through daily work routines. Too often, values and purpose statements remain glossy words published on corporate websites but are not felt and embodied in workplaces through people’s behaviours.

Building a culture of shared leadership is not easy. Especially in organisations with a long tradition of hierarchies and in a fast-paced, digitalised society where remote working is increasingly common and closing ourselves off in our own digital bubbles is fast becoming the norm. Building strong team rituals that cultivate deep relationships as well as support between team members and collective learning has become harder and is, nowadays, rather an exception than the norm. Such rituals demand a conscious effort that goes beyond yearly get-together meetings, and is sustained over time.

Formal managers often play an important role when a culture of shared leadership is being built, especially in the first phase as the organisation or team transitions away from traditional hierarchies. They must dare to break away from established patterns and norms and model another type of leadership, being courageous enough to open up, be vulnerable, and talk about their own challenges in the transformation journey. Managers need to actively let go of control and invite other colleagues to take up more space, assuming a more facilitative approach to leadership. This entails shifting from a parent-child dynamic in their relationship with colleagues towards an adult-adult dynamic. Sharing power and responsibility is not easy for managers who have built their whole career in a hierarchical setup.

What can help managers is adopting a practice of continuously inviting other colleagues into co-creation processes and facilitating them in a way that gives all team members the time and space they need to contribute. As part of these processes, the team can discuss and agree upon shared ways of working together, and establish regular team rituals. Team rituals should support the deepening of relationships and trust in the team while opening a forum for talks about challenges and conflicts, retrospectives on what’s going well and where there is space for development, as well as for discussing challenging topics like power. Holding space for team members to practise giving and receiving feedback and coaching each other is an important part of team rituals for shared leadership. Especially in the beginning, when team members are not well-versed in these practices, dedicating time and space for developing and practising feedback and coaching skills is necessary before they can be smoothly integrated into daily ways of working.

chapters.title: Changing roles and competencies for managers and employees

story.html: Over the last few months, elena has felt like something is shifting, slowly but genuinely. The open hour meetings. The honest conversations. But now, alone in her office, a question starts to haunt her: If my team doesn’t need me to have the answers, who am I?

For seven years, Elena had been the one who absorbed chaos from above and translated it into clarity below. The one who solved problems before they escalated. The one people would come to when they didn’t know what to do. That was her value. That was why she mattered. Even the changes she’d been making recently: the new meeting format, the honest feedback, the space she’d been trying to create. She had designed those. She had been the architect of openness. Which meant, she now realises uncomfortably, that she had still been in control of it.
Her phone buzzes: a message from her director requesting an update on the quarterly targets. kpis. She puts the phone face down.

Elena thinks about Jonas. Three months ago, after their conversation, something had reawakened in him. He’d started staying late again, not every day, but sometimes. The open hour had given his thinking a place to land. Watching this, she had felt something close to what she’d written down on the train: to see people become more than they thought they could be.

Elena decides to say nothing in the first open hour meeting. She won’t facilitate. Won’t redirect. She’ll just sit, notebook in lap, and see what happens when she steps back from being the gravitational centre of the room.

It is harder than she expected. The meeting begins without her usual whiteboard question. Jonas had volunteered to prepare something this week, partly as an experiment. He writes: What is one thing we’re doing for our care recipients that we’re proud of, and one thing we wish we could do differently?

They are good questions. The conversation moves. Sara talks about a family she’s been supporting through a difficult transition. Jamal tells a story about a care recipient who asked him, last week, whether anyone at the municipality actually reads the feedback forms. The room laughs, and then goes quiet. It isn’t really funny.
Elena grips her notebook. The question hangs in the air unanswered. The silence stretches. Every part of Elena wants to speak. Her mouth opens slightly.
She closes it. Jonas glances at her briefly, not for the answer, she thinks, but just to check. She gives the smallest shake of her head. Not yet.

Sara makes a connection that surprises her. Jamal builds on it. They begin discussing ways to make citizens participate more and what it means to be listened to. The direction that emerges is not the one Elena would have taken. She finds herself leaning forward slightly, genuinely interested in where this is going.
After the meeting, as people gather their things, Jonas stops beside her.

“You were quiet,” he says. “I was listening,” she replies. He nods. Then says, “It felt different. The room felt different.” Elena knows what he means. There had been a quality to the conversation: a kind of energy, people building upon each other rather than referring back to a centre. It was something she had not been able to manufacture when she was running things.

sections.title: Transitioning from fixed job descriptions to dynamic roles

blocks.html: In hierarchical organisations, managers are expected to make most of the decisions and are held accountable for a broad range of leadership activities such as planning and coordinating work, driving team performance, setting a vision, mediating conflict, coaching and developing employees, and supporting the different external and internal flows of communication, among others. While this model offers structure, it rests on the assumption that formal managers are capable of excelling across many different management tasks and dimensions of leadership. However, managers are human. And they bring their own strengths and limitations based on their personality, experience and background. Some are skilled at shaping team culture, building a positive atmosphere, and delivering honest feedback that is appreciated by employees. Other managers are natural motivators who are great at sharing a vision for the future of the group and possess the networking and presentation skills needed to represent the team in other parts of the organisation. However, expecting one person to lead across all these fronts and succeed at all of them places an unrealistic burden on the manager. Consequently, this implies that the team has growth potential that is still untapped.

Employees, on the other hand, are expected to fulfil tasks based on their job descriptions, which they were recruited for and which often change only once they are promoted. This way of dividing work into fixed roles has clear advantages: responsibilities are well-defined, accountability can be traced, and performance can be measured through key performance indicators (KPIs) linked to a specific job role. However, this “clarity” has negative consequences. For one thing, the full potential of employees is not explored and used. Team members with valuable skills, ideas, or interests that fall outside their formal job descriptions have little room to contribute to them. The consequence is that over time, these role boundaries limit employees’ development by reducing their freedom to explore new tasks and potentially making them feel they are not realising their full potential. The result can be a low level of engagement and sense of ownership among employees who become more passive and less likely to take initiative. Another reason why activating leadership potential and distributing leadership among employees and managers is important today is that teams and organisations are facing higher levels of complexity and uncertainty. In this context, collective leadership and intelligence are of great importance. One person can rarely make the best decision or find the best solution in a complex and unknown situation alone. It is more likely that what will make the team perform better is utilising collective intelligence and effort, with flexible and more fluid roles that allow different people to take the leadership role when their competence and experience are most needed. Distributing responsibility for tasks typically linked with the formal manager role allows the team to develop more leadership potential across its members and become more effective and adaptive, gaining the capacity to respond to various uncertain and complex situations by tapping into everyone’s leadership potential. Moving towards dynamic roles, therefore, enables teams to respond to constant change and work in more emergent and agile ways. It prevents employers from confining employees to specific boxes and labels. Instead, it increases autonomy and engagement, enabling employees to begin realising more of their potential.

In contrast to the traditional hierarchical model, leading together therefore involves redistributing many of the management responsibilities across the team. Instead of reassigning these tasks based on role title, team members can take them on based on their interests, relevant experience, and availability, given their current workload. This perspective on how to distribute managing tasks recognises that people perform best when their work life is balanced with their personal life. Sometimes, team members go through periods where personal circumstances make it difficult for them to perform their responsibilities. When leading together, a person experiencing a difficult situation in their personal life can temporarily step back from demanding tasks and instead take on ones that are easier or better fit their situation, such as tasks that can be done remotely or outside normal working hours. Once the person feels better, they can return to their usual responsibilities. This change in perspective has many benefits. To name a few: tasks are performed by people who are motivated and capable, team members grow through new challenges, people pursue their interests and benefit from higher levels of flexibility and well-being, and teams are more engaged and can adapt better to unforeseen challenges.

Moving from fixed to dynamic roles is a process that a team needs to navigate together. During our research project, we had the opportunity to work with Helen Triggs from The Hum. She describes dynamic roles as a structure that enables autonomy within clear guidelines: instead of one fixed job description, team members can have multiple roles. Such roles can be small or large, time-bound or ongoing, and can be transferred to another person when necessary. Roles are defined around outcomes (what needs to be achieved) rather than tasks, which means they set the goal rather than prescribing how to get there. This distinction is important because it gives team members the freedom to find their own way of doing things.

This dynamic approach to roles has a few core principles. The first one is Stewardship Over Ownership. It means that employees steward multiple roles rather than one job description and each role is linked to the work that needs to be done within that role rather than to a specific person. This makes a person steward a role during a specific period of time and then pass it on to another person, rather than owning it. Roles therefore become less vulnerable: different people can step in and out of them over different periods of time, and there is more flexibility in rotating them. The second principle of dynamic roles is Invitation Over Allocation. This means that it is not the formal manager who allocates responsibilities for different roles and tasks to team members, but rather there is a clear process in which people are invited to take on different roles, as well as a possibility for team members to suggest each other for specific roles. In this way, people are brought into roles through a conversation rather than assigned to roles from above.

Before a team can practise dynamic roles, they first need to define together which roles are needed to accomplish the work the team is doing, including those typically connected to the formal manager, such as championing purpose, coaching, and hosting team meetings. Each role is defined not by describing how one performs it, but rather through its purpose (why it exists and end result of doing it well) and its outcomes (broad outcomes that fulfil the purpose of the role, not tasks). For example, the coaching role is usually linked with formal managers and can be practised by any team member when distributing leadership within a team. The purpose of this role could be defined as “supporting others to be their best selves”, and the outcomes could be described as “coaching others and creating space for deep conversations”. Describing a role in this way makes what a team does more explicit and reduces conflict by defining clearer boundaries between roles. At the same time, it leaves a lot of space and autonomy for people to find their own ways of fulfilling the role.

If you would like to explore the rationale behind this transformation from fixed job descriptions to dynamic roles in greater depth, we recommend the series “Insights for the Journey”* by Frederic Laloux, author of the book Reinventing Organisations. And for a more concrete overview of how dynamic roles work in practice, we recommend the interview where Nati Lombardo speaks with Helen Triggs specifically on this topic: Dynamic Roles (youtube.com/watch?v=5hhuPwaYgHU). Finally, if your team is ready to begin mapping your own roles and experimenting with the process of distributing roles as a way of sharing responsibilities more fluidly, The Hum offers practical resources* and tools to support that process.

To test how it feels to share leadership in a more embodied way, moving away from the clear idea of the manager leading and employees following, try this movement exercise with your colleagues. Within a short time, you can experience a more fluid and emergent leadership dynamic, in which all team members continuously shift between leading and following until an emergent dynamic surfaces that makes it unclear who is leading and who is following. Together as a group, you develop a shared rhythm and a knowing of when to pause, when to move faster or slower and how to move seamlessly together through shared leadership.

Walk through a space and observe the shapes, colours and objects that you see. Find a detail you haven’t noticed before. Turn your gaze towards other people and look them in the eyes. Maintain awareness of your breathing. As you breathe out, release your neck, then your jaw, your feet. Release your weight to the ground. (5 min)

Shake hands with people and, as you do so, say your name. You can meet the same person multiple times. As you continue walking, follow another person by walking close by or far away, playing with distances. You are clear with where you are walking so that others can adjust their walk in relation to you. Do this for a few minutes before adding more layers to the walking.

If anyone in the room stops, we all stop. If anyone starts to walk, we all walk. Once stopped, take care that others have stopped before anyone starts walking again. Notice the whole space, all the people at once. (10 min)

Divide into teams of four and do the exact same exercise, but only follow your teammates. If any of your teammates stop or walk, everyone in the team follows. Travel through the space individually, meaning you don’t need to be close to your teammates. After a few minutes, notice the compositions that all the groups in the space create instantaneously. Do this for around 15 minutes.

In the following sections, we will see that the transformation towards leading together can be scary, requiring both employees and managers to step out of their comfort zones to reshape their roles and relationships with one another. This often necessitates the development of new skills and competencies.

sections.title: The evolving role of managers: from controlling outcomes to supporting co-creation processes

blocks.html: When an organisation begins moving towards leading together, the manager’s role is where the transformation is most felt and challenged. In traditional hierarchies, managers are expected to be in control of decisions, outcomes and direction. Shifting away from hierarchy makes managers feel like they need to change their identity because it asks them to step outside what has always felt like solid ground and learn to lead in a different way.

For the manager, the inner journey begins with understanding why leading together is important. Before anything else can change, managers need to make sense of what leading together means in practice: what does it look like on a normal Tuesday morning? Or during a difficult meeting where a project budget is cut in half? Learning about this requires consulting resources, such as this handbook or the ones you find throughout its chapters. From there, a natural step is opening up that conversation with the team: what values do we want to guide the way we work together? How do we want to distribute responsibility? The manager’s job is less about having the answers and more about creating the conditions for the team to find them together. This involves asking relevant questions, ensuring everyone is heard during meetings, and helping the group move through disagreement.

As the team begins experimenting, the manager’s attention shifts towards encouragement. This means inviting people to take on new responsibilities and step into leadership. Trusting that they can. Making that trust visible. It also means holding space for mistakes. People will experiment and try things that will not work. That is part of how they grow. A manager who steps in too quickly to fix things (however well-intended) is undermining the confidence they are trying to build.

When difficulties arise, the instinct to solve the problem directly is one of the hardest things to resist. But the more useful role is to help the team reflect: What happened? What did we learn? What might we try differently? This requires the manager to be patient, to believe that the team is capable of finding its own way through the problems.

Managers also play an active role in designing the rhythms and structures that help (and maintain) leading together: regular check-ins where people share what they need, retrospectives where the team steps back and reflects on how things are going. These activities are the spaces where leading together becomes real and the team can grow, as it is where the team develops the habits, the language, and the trust to take ownership.

Another responsibility is keeping the team connected to its purpose: reminding people and helping them navigate through questions of why they exist and what they care about. Another is helping team members get to know each other better – their skills, experience, and strengths – so that they can turn to each other directly when in need, instead of asking the manager.

And then there is the work that happens outside the team. Managers in hierarchical organisations often need to translate what their team is doing into language that makes sense to those above them. This can include advocating for the autonomy and resources the team needs, shielding them from pressures that could pull them back towards old ways of working, and bringing back useful feedback.

In our experience, including frequent interviews with managers, the most personal challenge is this: learning to let go. Trusting the process even when it feels slow. Sitting with uncertainty. Allowing the team to struggle without rushing to rescue them. This is uncomfortable in ways that are hard to anticipate. It asks managers to examine their own assumptions of what good leadership looks like. It also requires being honest with the team about the effort required, as the new skills and responsibilities needed will demand more from everyone, especially in the beginning.

sections.title: The evolving role of employees: learning to take initiative and responsibility

blocks.html: The shift towards leading together requires that employees step out of the roles where they often performed tasks defined by others and instead, become active co-creators of the team’s direction, processes and outcomes. This entails that team members expand their scope of responsibility, and it asks something of them: courage, new skills, and a willingness to keep growing.

The fundamental shift is learning to take initiative rather than wait for direction. In traditional hierarchical organisations, employees often have managers who set priorities and determine how work gets done. Leading together necessitates that team members proactively notice what needs attention, then propose solutions and bring ideas forward without waiting to be asked. This is about recognising when the team is facing something that calls for action from somebody, and then being willing to be that person. For many, that shift from reactive to proactive can feel unfamiliar and a little exposing, especially when the boundaries of the role have always been clearly drawn in the past. This process requires different forms of bravery as team members need to overcome self-doubt, be willing to be imperfect, and trust that colleagues will receive their efforts with generosity. It also means making peace with mistakes, viewing them as part of how people learn rather than as evidence that they should not have tried.

Leading together also means caring about the team as a whole, not just your own piece of the work. That includes noticing how colleagues are doing, whether the team is living up to its values, and being willing to speak up when something does not feel right, even when it would be easier to be silent or look the other way. This runs against many workplace cultures, where the pressure to appear competent can be too strong to resist. Leading together invites a different kind of presence: one where saying “I don’t know” or “I need help” is not a sign of weakness but an act of trust that makes collaboration possible.

There is also a very practical dimension to this shift that is easily overlooked. For a team to lead itself well, people need to stay curious about what their colleagues know, what they are good at, and what experience they bring. That shared picture of who knows what allows for the right person to step forward at the right moment, not because a manager directed them, but because the team has developed enough mutual awareness to recognise it together. This is something that needs continuous attention, as people grow and circumstances change.

It also helps to take a longer view of how this process unfolds. As employees grow more confident in leading collectively, the manager is naturally pulled away from the centre. This is a positive sign that leading together is working. However, the manager is still there and needs to care about maintaining the leading together perspective, as well as the structures, processes, culture, and the representation of the team outside of the team. What makes all of this possible is not a particular method or structure. It is people being willing to see themselves and each other differently: not as fixed roles doing what is in their job descriptions, but as individuals with great potential to contribute. The practitioners and artists we spoke to have each, in their own way, been working to create the conditions for this shift. And their experiences bring these ideas to life.

The shift from hierarchical leadership to leading together asks something from everyone involved, not just those at the top. The practitioners we spoke to have thought carefully about what it requires – both from the managers learning to let go and the employees learning to step up.

Karin Tenelius locates the starting point in something that seems simple: awareness. Most managers who operate in a parent-child dynamic with their employees don’t realise they are doing it. Neither do the employees. “It’s an invisible power, a hierarchical dynamic going on,” she says. In Sweden in particular, she observes that managers often believe they are coaching, involving and listening when, in practice, they are not. The theory is there; the behaviour has not followed. “So it’s an awakening.” And from awareness, she argues, comes the possibility of choice: the ability to notice the pattern you are in and decide, in that moment, to do something different. That choice requires honest feedback and straightforward interaction, catching yourself over and over again as old habits reassert themselves. At Tuff Leadership Training, where she and her colleagues have been self-organised for 23 years, they have developed a direct language for this. When someone slips into a passive or victim-like stance, a colleague might say: “We don’t have any employees here; we just have owners. Can you choose to be an owner? How would that sound?” It takes time, she says, especially for managers who have spent years in a different role. But it is learnable, through sustained practice and repeated choice.

Nati Lombardo approaches the same question from the manager’s perspective and offers something like a practical checklist for what genuine role modeling requires. It starts with showing up authentically: being willing to be vulnerable if you want others to be vulnerable, receiving feedback openly, and asking for it proactively rather than waiting for it to arrive. It means saying “I don’t know” when you do not know, making it visible that mistakes happen and that they are survivable, and holding yourself accountable if you want accountability to become a shared norm. “Those are probably some of the crucial pieces,” she says. Beyond that, it calls for making a real change to the way you occupy meetings and decisions: moving from directing to facilitating, from deciding to involving, from delegating tasks to opening up shared processes. “How do you involve others? How do you bring them into the conversation? How do we encourage shared decision-making or shared delegation?” For employees who are more used to a traditional passive role, Nati is honest about the challenge. Change on that side of the relationship is harder to sustain if the people with formal power have not shifted first. “You first need the leaders and the people in power to shift out of their current perspective, their roles, or their ways of doing things, to model something different, so that others can pick it up and start doing it as well. Otherwise, you can talk as much as you want.” Given that foundation, she points to a few practices that can help employees grow into more active participation. Learning facilitation skills is one, not only because it equips people to run meetings but because the act of facilitating is itself a form of stepping into leadership. “It gives you a sense of empowerment, a sense of: I can also do something that is leading the team towards some outcome.” Proactively asking for feedback is another practice she recommends, as it helps build self-awareness and opens space for the kinds of difficult conversations that most teams find hard to sustain.

One practice Nati returns to with particular enthusiasm is what she calls pods: small peer coaching groups of three to five people who meet regularly, usually every two weeks, specifically to support each other’s development. The groups are deliberately composed across different parts of the organisation, bringing together people who do not normally work together, which gradually strengthens the social fabric of the organisation. They are rotated every six months or so, so that trust and relationships keep building in new directions. What happens in a session varies by team and by moment. Sometimes someone brings a specific challenge they want to think through together. Sometimes it is more of a check-in: how are you feeling, what are you struggling with, what do you need? Some pods use more structured formats – like Troika from Liberating Structures1 or Case Clinic from Theory U2 – for delving deeper into something. Others keep it more conversational. Sometimes the focus is tied to a specific developmental goal a person is working on. “If that person is currently focused on bringing more appreciation into the team, the focus of the meetings will be on that developmental goal and how they’re doing.” Sometimes it is as immediate as: “I just need feedback on this presentation I’m preparing.”
1. To find out more, check out: liberatingstructures.com/8-troika-consulting/
2. To find out more, check out: u-school.org/caseclinic

What Nati finds significant about the pods model is what it replaces and supplements. The standard HR procedure of a once-or-twice-a-year developmental talk between a manager and an employee, with a few followup meetings scattered throughout the year, leaves people without the kind of continuous, in-time support that actually helps them grow. A manager responsible for 20 or even 50 people cannot realistically be the primary source of assessing their performance and knowing what development is needed for each employee. “I have no idea what they all do in everyday operations, so I cannot be the main and only person evaluating their performance and helping them develop,” as one manager she worked with put it. Peer coaching, distributed across the organisation and built into regular rhythms, begins to fill that gap. And in doing so, it shifts the culture: from one where development is something steered for you by someone above you, to one where it is something you and your colleagues are actively doing together.

In most organisations, a manager’s role comes with a very clear “score”. There are expectations about how to occupy a room, how much to speak, where to stand, and what to know. Managers are expected to have the answers, to perform and be competent, and to be the central presence in meetings. Their schedules reflect this: dense with meetings – occasions to demonstrate that they are managing others. In the workshops he facilitated, Dejan Srhoj proposed something that goes directly against all of this. What if managers became listening structures instead? What if they spent time simply hanging around the kitchen, observing with their whole body, entering meetings only when invited, attending to what was actually happening around them rather than performing their role at the front of the room?

The proposal sounds simple. What it asks of people is considerable, because the role is not just a set of behaviours. It is, as Dejan describes it, a score that people inhabit so completely that they become it. “A lot of what we do is: we perform our job role, and the role has a quite clear set of instructions. And the moment you find yourself in it, suddenly you become this role.” What dance and choreography do to make this visible is they invite people to shift perspective, to move differently in the room, and to relate to others from an unfamiliar position in which the role and the person are not the same thing. The role demands certain behaviours, but there is space, always, for negotiation between what is expected and how you actually inhabit it. We just need to provide a rehearsal ground for practising other ways of being with each other.

When that space opens up, something changes in how people are viewed and view themselves. Employees who had been silent through entire workshops began, over time, to facilitate, to propose, to lead. In one case, a person who had said almost nothing in the early sessions ended up reading a poem to a room of politicians and moving them to tears. The shift of power was not announced or planned. It emerged as people encountered themselves and each other outside the positions their roles had assigned them. “By shifting roles, or by inviting people to change perspectives, or how they see things, or how they are in the room, how they relate to others, we get different aspects and qualities of the people, and see them as individuals that have their own perks and qualities, which are different from the role that they are expected to fulfil or embody.” What becomes possible then are relations that are fuller, more trusting, more capable of genuine dialogue and even criticism, because the people in them are no longer being taken as monolithic structures but as dynamic, emerging processes. Dejan is careful about how he views managers. He does not experience them as powerful beings who could change things but choose not to. He experiences them as people under enormous and rarely acknowledged pressure, caught between the desires and needs of the people below them and the expectations and demands of the people above them, constrained from every side, and often privately longing for exactly the kind of playfulness and flexibility they are not supposed to show. “At the end of the day, you are also just a human being who also maybe wants to be playful and not give a damn, but you’re not allowed to. Or you don’t allow yourself, because you think you’re not allowed.” These restrictions he describes are real, and they are structural. What the workshops try to do, at their best, is create a temporary suspension of that structure: a space where a manager can spend a day performing as an employee, or as someone deeply critical of everything, and where an employee who has never led anything can suddenly be the one creating a choreography and discovering what it actually takes.

The invitation, ultimately, is not to blame individuals for the roles they play but to look honestly at what produces those roles. “Let’s not assume that they are simply very stiff beings afraid of change. Let’s assume that they actually want change. Let’s assume that they are not stiff, and let’s look at what does not allow them to be playful or flexible. Let’s look at the structural context to see why they are like they are.” That shift in framing, from judging people to examining the systems that shape them, is one of the quieter but more consequential things that artistic practice, with its attention to how roles are constructed and inhabited, brings to the work of leading together.

This tool is used to help people reflect on how they could expand their current job role by trying out new roles, through which they can contribute to shared leadership in their team or organisation. The first section of the Re-thinking My Role Canvas asks you to reflect on the different new roles you could assume to contribute to leading together, defining the purpose of these new roles. The second section invites you to reflect on the challenges and development opportunities that come with the new roles through which you think you could contribute to shared leadership. The last one invites you to visualise what the signs of success would be–evidence that you are performing these new roles well and contributing to shared leadership in your team or organisation.

sections.title: Competencies needed for managers and employees

blocks.html: A practical tool for rethinking your current job role through the lens of your desired contribution to shared leadership.

Leading together requires developing skills that are often not rewarded in traditional hierarchical settings or taught in a typical classroom or university course. These skills are often difficult for the untrained eye to notice. They are usually skills developed through practice, experimentation, awareness and reflection on the dynamics that emerge when working with others. We have compiled an initial list of these skills, including listening, dialogue, navigating conflict, giving and receiving feedback, coaching, daring to be vulnerable at work and facilitation. In this section, we provide an overview and highlight some related resources worth exploring.
For those who want to explore this further, Scharmer’s u.lab is an initial resource we recommend visiting: presencing.org/theoryu

Listening is perhaps the most underestimated. Obviously, it is not only about hearing what someone is saying. Otto Scharmer, the creator of Theory U*, describes four levels of listening that illustrate the extent to which this skill can be developed. The first is downloading. This happens when you listen while confirming what you already think, filtering everything through your own experience. The second is fac-tual listening, when you are able to notice what is new or different in what someone says. The third is empathic listening, when you are able to shift perspectives to see the world through the other person’s eyes. The fourth, which Scharmer calls generative listening is the one hardest to acquire: a quality of presence where something new can emerge that neither person could have arrived at alone. Most of us spend more time than we realise at the first level. Moving towards the deeper ones is a practice. Another resource to check out is the Vuslat Foundation and their concept of Generous Listening*: listening not just as a way to understand, but as an act of genuine care and attention towards the other person. It involves listening to yourself, to others and to nature.
generouslistening.org/

Closely connected to listening is the skill of dialogue. This means being able to host conversations where the goal is not to convince but to explore. Where you can remain open to having your mind changed, and where disagreement is treated as something useful and appreciated. This skill is harder to cultivate in cultures that value having the right answer.
In Chapter 3, “Transforming culture and the way we relate to each other”, you can find more information and suggestions for practising listening and dialogue.

Navigating conflict well becomes more important as more people become involved in shaping the direction and making decisions. More voices naturally means more friction. It is part of how teams think together. Learning how to express disagreement respectfully, stay present when things get uncomfortable, and work through tension are vital qualities to develop.

Coaching and giving feedback have traditionally been associated with managers. However, in a team that leads together, these skills are also shared among members. Supporting a colleague’s development, asking a good question at the right moment, offering an honest observation or coaching support are all practices that help the team take care of itself and keep learning. What matters just as much is receiv-ing feedback – cultivating openness and approaching feedback with curiosity rather than defensiveness. You can find more tips on coaching and feedback in Chapter 3.

Vulnerability is about having the courage to say “I don’t know”, asking for help and admitting when something is not working. In many organisations, these things have been treated as signs of weakness, and people are often scared to practise them. Leading together asks people to unlearn that, and to discover that being honest about uncertainty or a tough situation you are going through is often what opens up the most meaningful and productive dialogues. Being vulnerable means having the courage to share intimate and vulnerable things about yourself that you might not dare to reveal in a hierarchical and performance-driven organisation. For example, sharing that you are stressed because you have been spending a lot of your time worrying and taking care of your child or parent with health issues, which has resulted in you not being able to focus at work or devote the time and energy others expect you to.

And then there are facilitation skills. These are about creating the conditions needed for meaningful conversation and co-creation. They also involve helping to maintain focus on the purpose of a meeting or workshop and helping ensure that all voices are heard. Facilitation means helping a group converge when their voices are too fragmented, going in different directions, or diverge; when everyone is stuck in existing ways of thinking and becoming too complacent with the status quo. We were surprised to discover that not many of the managers in our projects had the skills needed to facilitate co-creation within their teams. Furthermore, many employees would benefit from developing these skills. Some organisations participating in our projects have therefore actively invested in sending people from across their organisation to facilitation courses. Anyone can develop these skills through practice.
artofhosting.org
dianemushohamilton.com

If you want to learn more, you can explore the Art of Hosting* community, a global network of people interested in applying facilitation through participatory methods in different organisational contexts. Two other practical resources we recommend are books. One is the Swedish book Facilitera! (Facilitate!), featuring a lot of facilitation exercises written by Anna Gullstrand. The other one is the Facilitator’s Guide to Participatory Decision-Making, a practical book by Sam Kaner that helps groups develop shared understandings. Diane Musho Hamilton* is also a master facilitator and award-winning mediator whose courses we found useful for further developing facilitation skills.

Lastly, underlying some of the core competencies for leading together, we cannot forget about self-leadership: knowing yourself well enough to understand your own reactions, set boundaries and to act in ways that are consistent with what you care about. As we have written before, the personal transformation journey is a crucial element in the transformation process from hierarchies towards collective forms of leadership. This competency is so important that it deserves a whole chapter – so, learn more about it in Chapter 2. Unless they develop their self-leadership competencies, both managers and employees will struggle to transform their own roles and change their behaviours.

In both Denmark and Sweden, the law requires that every employee have a person formally responsible for their workplace. That legal reality means that in the public sector, the question has never been whether to remove managers, but rather how their role needs to change. Mette Aagaard has spent years working with this question, and her answer is grounded in what she calls the hybrid model: an organisational design where formal leadership structures continue to exist alongside distributed decision-making. Here, the challenge is learning to make both work together without one undermining the other.

The clearest example she draws on is a child welfare NGO in Denmark with around 250 employees. Mette has followed them closely, and their approach, work, and impact formed an important part of the research for her own book on shared leadership*. They started their journey in 2018 and have persistently continued to develop their own model. The way they explain it is through a spatial metaphor. The traditional organisational structure, the reporting lines, the formal manager, the place where someone assesses how you are doing and whether you have access to development, is what they call “the place where you live”. It is where you feel a sense of connectedness, where someone holds responsibility for your well-being and growth. The circles, the distributed decision-making structures, they call “the place where you go to work”. The two serve different purposes and neither replaces the other.
djoefforlag.dk/products/medledelse

Within that model, the role of the formal manager shifts considerably. At “home”, the manager’s job is to maintain an ongoing dialogue with each employee: asking how they are doing, if anything is standing in the way of them feeling committed and able to thrive, and whether there are conflicts that need addressing. Checking whether the base is safe. When it comes to the work, the manager’s role is to ensure that mandates are clear, that aims are well-defined, and that decision-making authority is genuinely distributed rather than just nominally so. If two teams are struggling to coordinate, the manager does not step in and solve it. Rather, the manager creates the conditions for the people involved to solve it themselves. “My role would be to invite that dialogue, but not to solve the problem. To facilitate, to keep the dialogue open, not jump into solution mode right away.” There is even a phrase for the temptation to do otherwise: “stealing decisions”. Once you have given the right to decide to someone else, you cannot come and take it back. “You have to keep them there.”

However, certain responsibilities remain with top management. Strategy, for instance, is still the responsibility of senior leaders, even if others should be involved in it. What’s important is the overall shift in the manager’s role – from the go-to fix-it person to a facilitator of dialogue, decision-making, and exploration.

According to Mette, what this shift requires goes deeper than a set of new skills. There is thinking that needs to be unlearned before new thinking can take root, and it operates at such a subconscious level that making it conscious is the necessary first step. One held assumption she often works to dismantle is the belief that consensus is the foundation of all good decision-making, and that when consensus cannot be reached, the manager must step in and decide. Replacing that assumption requires developing a genuinely different relationship to disagreement: the capacity to refrain from using whatever formal or informal power you hold to push your own preferences through, and to stay in a mode of exploration rather than resolution. “It’s perfectly fine that I don’t agree with you. I don’t need to agree with you in order for us to move forward and explore and improve and execute.” That is not primarily a skill, she says. It is a fundamental belief which, once understood and held, gradually translates into action and eventually becomes a skill.

The same logic applies to what Mette calls the dance between managers and employees, a dynamic she has seen play out in every organisation she has worked with. The steps are familiar: an employee notices something that is not working and reports it to the manager, and both parties operate from the shared assumption that it is the manager’s job to fix it. If the manager does not act, the employee is entitled to complain. And managers, she says, largely accept this arrangement, feeling the full weight of a responsibility that is both isolating and structurally impossible to discharge well. “If someone tells me two colleagues cannot collaborate, or an employee looks completely exhausted, or a department can’t make sense of a recent change, I feel it’s 100% my responsibility to fix it. That leaves managers in a very lonely place, but also a very inefficient one, because we are very rarely able to solve these kinds of issues alone.”

The dance becomes a blaming cycle. Managers want employees to take more responsibility for the shared workplace and grow frustrated when they do not. Employees feel ready to take responsibility but find that without a real mandate, their initiative leads nowhere. “It’s only if he or she agrees with me that my responsibility can actually be used for anything.” Both sides are right about the other, and neither can move without the other moving first.

The shift Mette is pointing towards calls for a replacement of that whole dynamic with something different: the idea that whatever occurs is a shared responsibility, and that simply naming a problem does not fulfil your part of it. “I offer my willingness to come up with ideas. I offer my collegial support regardless of whether you are a manager, an employee, or a colleague. We need to figure out what we can do together.” It sounds straightforward when stated plainly. She is honest: getting it to work in practice is something else entirely.
